- A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never act *on* the shared checkout while a background agent is live in it, either: don't amend a commit the subagent already pushed, and don't relay a "fix" instruction built from a misread of its in-flight state. If the checkout-back or the corrective action is itself refused by the session's own permission classifier, that refusal is the tell — a live subagent is using the checkout — so don't retry or force it; leave the branch alone and wait for the subagent to finish.
- Once a source is delegated to a background subagent, reading or re-analyzing it yourself while the dispatch is running is wasted work, not a safety net. A subagent dispatched to mine one file, log, or page fully owns it, and the orchestrator's own parallel read of the same source computes nothing the subagent doesn't already report — it only burns tool calls and wall-clock alongside a dispatch that will hand back the same findings anyway. Wait on the dispatch with no tool call, or spend the interim on genuinely different work; read the subagent's report when it lands rather than re-deriving it in parallel.
- Before concluding a lost background subagent "made no progress" — its handle went unreachable after a genuine worker restart, and you need to decide whether to relaunch — check every channel it could have written to, not only git state and the dispatch thread's own comments. A subagent can produce real output through a channel a narrow recovery check doesn't think to look at (filing its own tracking issue, for one, moments before it went down), and checking only git log/status plus the parent conversation's comments reads as "nothing survived" when something did. Relaunching a fresh subagent from scratch on that false premise duplicates the lost one's work. Search broadly — issues, PRs, comments — across the write surface a subagent could have used before declaring nothing landed.
- Catching a flawed prompt or input right after dispatching a background subagent — send a follow-up message to *that same* agent to resume it, never a fresh redispatch over the identical source. A redispatch runs a full second pass in parallel with the first, at full cost, even when the original would have handled the flaw fine on its own or needs only a small correction. Prefer pointing a subagent at a reference file's *path* to read for itself over pasting its content inline in the prompt, too — cheaper, and immune to the class of bug where the pasted content is left as an unfilled placeholder.

lines: - **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.

- When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.

- A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.

## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search

A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.

input.new_string:
A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.

The asymmetry cuts the other way too: a tool that takes an explicit `owner`/`repo` argument naming a repo *outside* your scope is refused outright — denied, not silently filtered — which is the safe, expected behaviour. Never chain a `-f` pkill; bracket a character (`"[h]ttp.server 8099"`) to break the self-match. | | GoogleCalendarEventCreator | `git-github-advanced` (new section) | `git checkout -- ` writes ``'s committed tree over the working copy, unrecoverably destroying the uncommitted edits it was reached for. Branch in place, or commit/stash first. | | EdFringeNow | `git-github-advanced` (new section) | Probe an egress-blocked host from a hosted runner: a small probe script plus a path-filtered push-triggered workflow, read from job logs, both deleted before the PR. | | GoogleCalendarEventCreator | `packs/basics/RULES.md` | No pack prose + no owner preferences + no between-turn check feedback is the tell that the SessionStart hook didn't fire — re-run it instead of reading it as "this project has no rules". | | TLDR | `generate-project-instructions` skill | A pack homes *how we work*; a statement of what the product **does** is a requirement belonging to the executable spec and its suite, not to a pack (canon or local). Pack-worthiness is a question about the work, not about how load-bearing the code is. | | VascularColoring | `packs/research-project/RULES.md` §1 | An annotation overlay never uses a colour the signal itself carries (it vanishes exactly on the objects it marks), and it must show where the method breaks, as explicit checkable claims. | | HelloWorldFlutterApp | `packs/flutter/RULES.md` | Don't commit `pubspec.lock` churn from a local `flutter pub get` — a locally installed SDK resolves differently from CI's, so it is version skew, not a dependency change. | **Prose-fallback reason (all seven):** no repo-state signature a check could carry. ```markdown
## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `leaflet/tile-attribution` | critical | legal | check: blocking |
```

- **Rule** — a name, under 8 words: enough to find the rule, never a summary of it. **Check** — its id.
- **Severity** — the consequence of ignoring it: `critical` (ships a defect to users, loses data,
  breaks the fleet, or violates a licence or platform policy), `high` (the work lands wrong or
  silently doesn't work and someone must redo it), `medium` (rework or drift caught inside the
  repo), `low` (friction only).
- **Reason** — the kind of cost: `correctness`, `performance`, `complexity`, or `legal` (licence,
  privacy, disclosure, store or platform policy). One per rule, the dominant one.
- **Enforcement** — the mechanism and its price. `prose: <n> words` is what the rule *costs*: every
  declaring repo pays those words in every session's context, counted by
  [`../engine-tests/rule-index.mjs`](../engine-tests/rule-index.mjs). `check: blocking | advisory` is
  how the engine reports a finding. A rule carried both ways names the check too.

Neither table describes what a rule says — the prose and the check's own failure message do that.

Both indexes are held to the tree by [`../engine-tests/rule-index.test.mjs`](../engine-tests/rule-index.test.mjs):
the rows must match `RULES.md` one-for-one with the right word counts, every check the pack runs must
appear, and both vocabularies are closed. That guard is what makes a second listing of the rules safe
here — an earlier hand-kept index drifted into claiming a prose rule that never existed (#777) — so
recount a rule's row in the same change that edits its prose, and add a check's row in the change
that declares it.

## Pack badge (`badge`)

Every pack carries a mark — the 32×32 tile beside its name in the table above — so a repo's README
can show which Claudinite packs it runs. It is `badge.svg` beside the pack's manifest, found by
convention rather than named by it (above).

**The badge file is the artwork's source of truth.** Its colour and its glyph live in the SVG, not
in `pack.mjs`: they are visible to anyone who opens the file, editable without touching a manifest,

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
reports it.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |

## Checks

Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |

What goes wrong when one fires:

- `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-settings.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` barrier edge).
- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.

The **task contract** and its checks are deliberately NOT here. Those ask whether a task is
*written* correctly, which is authoring; every check above asks whether Claudinite is *working* in
this repo. They live with the rest of the authoring surface.

The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays with the other
doc-integrity rules.

## Skills

| Skill | For |
|---|---|
| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

The adoption skills bundle two more checks of the same kind, over the answers a member stores
against each declared pack's questions:

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `adoption-answers-pending` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `interview-answer-stale` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

## Tasks

| Task | frequency | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `update` | daily (02:00 anchor) | the mount is behind the canon, or a declared pack moved |
| `adopt-requested-packs` | daily | the repo carries an open pack-adoption request |

`update` is the per-repo self-refresh — the task that converges a member's mount and stamps it. It
is why `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` is blocking: a member runs `update` from its **vendored** copy, and
`discoverTasks` finds only a literally-declared pack's tasks, so a repo that loses this pack's entry
loses its self-refresh, and nothing is left that could deliver it one. That is also why the task
arrived here a change later than the rest of the pack — it moved only once every non-dormant member's
declaration had been read back and confirmed to carry `core`.

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
reports it.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |
| Finding a canon fix while working in a member | high | correctness | prose: 120 words |
| A file referenced but absent from the vendor set | medium | correctness | prose: 93 words |
| Pushing a change to workflows or pack config | medium | correctness | prose: 57 words |

## Checks

Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |

What goes wrong when one fires:

- `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-settings.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` barrier edge).
- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.

The **task contract** and its checks are deliberately NOT here. Those ask whether a task is
*written* correctly, which is authoring; every check above asks whether Claudinite is *working* in
this repo. They live with the rest of the authoring surface.

The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays with the other
doc-integrity rules.

## Skills

| Skill | For |
|---|---|
| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

The adoption skills bundle two more checks of the same kind, over the answers a member stores
against each declared pack's questions:

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `adoption-answers-pending` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `interview-answer-stale` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

## Tasks

| Task | frequency | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `update` | daily (02:00 anchor) | the mount is behind the canon, or a declared pack moved |
| `adopt-requested-packs` | daily | the repo carries an open pack-adoption request |

`update` is the per-repo self-refresh — the task that converges a member's mount and stamps it. It
is why `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` is blocking: a member runs `update` from its **vendored** copy, and
`discoverTasks` finds only a literally-declared pack's tasks, so a repo that loses this pack's entry
loses its self-refresh, and nothing is left that could deliver it one. That is also why the task
arrived here a change later than the rest of the pack — it moved only once every non-dormant member's
declaration had been read back and confirmed to carry `core`.

input.body:
Growth-promote run over the two target members named in #1435's Context: **ClaudiniteWebsite** and **Shepherd**.

### Promoted (10)

| Origin | Rung | Landed | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| ClaudiniteWebsite | prose | `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md` | Finding a fix that belongs in the canon while working in a member repo: the scratch clone is read-only in practice (fetch works, push 403s) — that's org egress policy, not a bug to route around. Patch it as a diff on an issue in the member repo, never push, and never edit the vendored mount in place. |
| ClaudiniteWebsite | prose | `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md` | A file a vendored module references but that's absent from `.claudinite/shared/` is evidence about the vendor *set*, not the canon — check the canon itself before filing an issue claiming it was never shipped. |
| Shepherd | prose | `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md` | Before pushing a change that touches workflows, `.claudinite-checks.json`, or pack config, run `check_the_world.mjs` locally — it's the same script CI's conformance job runs. |
| Shepherd | prose | `packs/basics/RULES.md` (Harness-tool contracts) | Check whether `AskUserQuestion`'s answer is already decided before reaching for it, and batch every open decision into one call rather than asking serially. |
| Shepherd | prose | `packs/basics/RULES.md` (Harness-tool contracts) | Waiting on a subagent/task with nothing left to do — say so in plain text with no tool call; a manufactured no-op can come back with no visible text and force an interrupt. |
| ClaudiniteWebsite | prose (sharpen) | `unattended-agents` skill | Sharpens the shared-checkout rule: never amend a subagent's already-pushed commit or relay a fix instruction built from a misread of its in-flight state; if the checkout-back or the fix is itself refused by the permission classifier, that refusal is the tell a live subagent is using the checkout — don't force it. |
| ClaudiniteWebsite + Shepherd (independently) | prose | `unattended-agents` skill | Once a source is delegated to a background subagent, reading/re-analyzing it yourself while it runs is wasted work, not a safety net — wait on the dispatch or spend the interim elsewhere. |
| ClaudiniteWebsite | prose | `unattended-agents` skill | Before declaring a lost background subagent "made no progress" after a worker restart, check every channel it could have written to (issues, PRs, comments), not only git state and the dispatch thread's own comments. |
| Shepherd | prose | `unattended-agents` skill | Catching a flawed prompt right after dispatching a background subagent — resume it with a follow-up message, never a fresh redispatch over the identical source. |
| Shepherd | prose | `git-github-advanced` skill (sharpen + 2 new) | Sharpens the repo-allowlist rule with the scoped-vs-scopeless asymmetry (a repo-argument tool is denied outright when out of scope; a scopeless one like `search_code`/`search_issues` isn't and can still leak). Adds: `search_code`'s index can lag and undercount for an exhaustive enumeration; a multi-target sweep should `subscribe_pr_activity` on every PR it leaves open, not a sample. |

**Prose for all ten** — every one is in-flight judgment (which tool to reach for, whether to shadow a subagent, how to read a denial) or a tool/platform behavioral caveat with no repo-state signature a check could carry. No conformance-backlog issues opened.

### Notable rejections — already covered (dedup)

- ClaudiniteWebsite's "site describes itself in prose beyond its privacy claims" — already the general shape of `basics/RULES.md`'s "grep the whole surface for the standing absolutes it touches" (Changing what you do with user data).
- ClaudiniteWebsite's `converge-item.mjs` step-6 failure mode — superseded: the current `queue/instructions.md` step 6 already handles this exact case (the `CLAUDINITE_ITEM_REPO`/`CLAUDINITE_ITEM_JSON` replay path).
- Shepherd's "hunting for the standing tracker issue by exact title" — `git-github-advanced` already carries this in full (`in:title` + semantic-match caveat + list-and-match-yourself).
- Shepherd's "don't guess a PR/issue number you're about to create" — already implied by `unattended-agents`' "resolve every value before the comment goes up… same for every PR number, sha and label."
- Shepherd's "cap and qualify every list/search call" and its GitHub-MCP-overflow items — already carried by `git-github-advanced`'s existing bound-and-qualify section.
- Shepherd's "scratchpad filename collisions across parallel dispatch" — already an existing `unattended-agents` bullet, verbatim in shape.
- Shepherd's various git/branch mechanics (shallow-checkout `merge-base`, `origin/main` staleness, PR-by-branch-name lookup, squash-merge cleanup) — already covered by existing `git-github-advanced` sections.

**Deferred, not promoted:** Shepherd's "declaring a repo as the store for a role a retiring predecessor filled — copy the actual content in the same change" is a real, somewhat narrower pattern; left for a future pass rather than stretched to fit this run's bar.

Closes no issue (a scheduled run, not a feature) — Refs #1435.
